newsitem.title: UK: Traders see imminent Iraqi oil, too late for some.
newsitem.headline: Traders see imminent Iraqi oil, too late for some.

text.p: Some of Baghdad's closest oil trading allies were confident on Wednesday that Iraqi crude exports are set to resume shortly.
But traders said Iraq marketers may struggle to find buyers in the key Mediterranean market where many delay-weary traders have opted to meet their August requirements with other grades.
Not a drop of Iraqi oil has been exported under the third 90 day term, beginning June 8, of the United Nations oil-for-food agreement.
Some potential buyers said they have given up hope of any sales at all before the next period commences in early September.
But trading sources in touch with Baghdad's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) said on Wednesday that they believed flows would resume much sooner.
"We see things escalating in the next seven days to the point at which we'll have exports," said one.
Oil exports have been delayed by nearly two months due to Iraq's insistence that the U.N. first approved a new plan for distributing aid.
The U.N. said on Tuesday that it was optimistic that its review of the plan can be completed by the end of the week, clearing the way for Secretary-General Kofi Annan to give his approval.
Some traders said that the process of agreeing price formulas and signing contracts could be sewn up quickly after that.
Buyers with contracts under the first six-months of sales won't be required to make the long road trip to Baghdad to renew contracts, they said.

"It can be as quick as 24 hours (for contracts to be renewed). We won't have to go to Baghdad. All the original signed documents will stand -- including adjustments," said one regular lifter in the first round of sales.
Under the terms of the U.N. agreement, Iraq is allowed to sell up to $2 billion other six months in two 90 day instalments to buy food and medicines.
If exports do resume by the start of the second week in August, Iraq looks unlikely to be able to reach its $1 billion revenue target by the end of the current 90 day period on September 5.

At current prices, exports would have to hit two million barrels per day (bpd), although traders say that export capacity is currently just 1.3 million bpd -- 700,000 bpd at the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan and 600,000 bpd at Mina al Bakr in the Gulf.
Actual export capacity, which Iraq publicly puts nearer two million barrels daily, will remain a mystery until fully tested.
World markets may find such a flood of barrels hard to soak up, particularly after countless delays have bred scepticism among many traders that exports would resume at all in August.
In the Mediterranean sour market, refiners have keenly bought up August-loading cargoes of Russian Urals, the main alternative sour grade.
The August programme is now sold out until the last decade, with the rush of buying hiking the price to a high of Dated Brent -55 cents, the smallest midsummer discount for several years.

"People are wondering whether (the Iraqis) are going to bother with the first 90 days at all. A lot of them have made sure they are covered almost up until the end of the month," said a trader for a major European refiner.
Sales to the Far East may also be difficult because of the long nomination periods for loading that Asian buyers require.
Iraq's Japanese customers in the first round of sales, though, may have reserved a gap for Iraqi cargoes.
Those who have ruled out the possibility of Iraqi sales may kick themselves if exports do resume soon.
Most in the market expect the price formula for European sales to remain unchanged from the first six months.

The formula links the price to Arab Light crude, and assuming differentials remain the same, the August price of Kirkuk would be Dated Brent -$2.00, or equivalent to around Dated Brent -$1.50/41.40 on a delivered basis.
"You expect a bit of a discount for Kirkuk against Urals, but anyone can see that's extremely competitive the way the levels are now," said one trader.
--R Russell, S Hayden, London newsroom 542 5387
